To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the EMX2 gradient persists in the developing human neocortex; (2) the gradient is similar to that seen in rodents, suggesting that it may play a role in arealization; and (3) the PAX6, NEUROG, TBR2 and TBR1 gradients are lost during development, which suggests that the PAX6 gradient is not involved in specifying areal identity.

the expression of EMx2 and PAX6 mRNA is restricted to the proliferating zones and that the expression of TBR1, NEUROG2 and TBR2 mRNA is restricted to progenitors and immature neurons, and is lost as cells mature.

(i) EMX2 mRNA is expressed in the VZ, SVZ and cortical plate in the human neocortex, unlike the rodent; and (ii) the gradients of expression of PAX6 and the corticoneurogenic genes TBR2, NeuroD, and TBR1 are lost early in corticogensis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the human cortex, which has been studied in great detail in rodents, but is poorly understood in humans.
the development of the human cortex and the molecular mechanisms involved in the formation of its arealization and cytoarchitecture, and the role of the gene EMX2 in this process.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the formation of cortical arealization, and how this is affected by the genetic and environmental factors that influence human brain evolution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while EMX2 expression is restricted to progenitors, PAX6 is expressed by all progenitors, and TBR2, NeuroD, and TBR1 are sequentially expressed in cells as they leave the proliferative zone.

, while there are some similarities in the expression patterns of the genes studied in the human and rodent, there is a clear difference in the spatio‐temporality of their expression, with the human cortex being more advanced than that of the rodents.
EMX2 is involved in the specification of the neocortex, while PAX6 is involved in the regulation of the radial glial lineage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression patterns of the transcription factors analysed are not identical in the human and rodent cortex, however the gradients of expression are very similar.

, although EMX2 and PAX6 expression in the human neocortex is similar to that in the mouse, the expression of genes that are downstream of PAX6 is less restricted to specific cortical compartments, and that these gradients disappear earlier in human than in rodent development.
the expression gradients of EMX2 and PAX6 are more similar to that of rodents than TBR2, NeuroD or TBR1.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the expression of PAX6 mRNA in the human VZ and SVZone is not sufficient to specify rostral identity, and that the loss of PAX 6, TBR 2, NEU RO D and TBR 1 mRNA gradients in the developing human neocortex may correlate with the translocation of EM X2 mRNA to the cortical plate, which is not seen in the rodents.

, although gradients of gene expression are lost early in corticogenetic development, the genes involved in the establishment of these gradients are expressed in a manner that is consistent with the rodent.

the gradients of PAX6 and TBR2, which are involved in corticoneuronal specification, are not maintained during corticogenesis in the human, and that this is not the case for the EMX2 gradient, which is maintained throughout corticogenesis.
